classifications.reasoning: The rule detects a spoofed Host header pattern ('.com-') used by the Nuclear exploit kit to impersonate legitimate domains, which is a form of protocol or service impersonation.
The rule matches HTTP traffic to a known Harakit botnet C2 domain (sousi.extasix.com) and URI (/genst.htm), directly observing command-and-control over web protocols.
The rule identifies requests for executable files (exe, dll, scr, etc.) from WordPress 'wp-content' directories, indicating ingress tool transfer from a compromised site.
The rule flags a specific malicious User-Agent string (Opera/10) used by malware for C2 communication over HTTP.
The rule detects a Kazy/FakeAV check-in pattern: a specific URI (/images/m.php?id=), an outdated IE6 User-Agent, and missing Referer header, all indicative of C2 over web protocols.
Similar to the previous rule, this matches a different URI path (/ccbill/m.php?id=) with the same IE6 User-Agent and no Referer, showing C2 traffic.
The rule only spots an iframe containing 'config.inc.php' in HTTP responses, which is an indicator of compromise but does not directly reveal a specific ATT&CK technique observable on the network.

The rule matches Medfos Trojan C2 traffic: a distinct URI (/feed?req=http), an IE User-Agent, missing Accept-Language and Referer headers, and an IP address in the Host header, all characteristic of HTTP-based command and control.
The rule looks for the string 'PCRatd' in HTTP traffic, which is associated with PCRat backdoor data uploads, i.e., exfiltration over the C2 channel.
The rule detects HTTP parameters (hostid, hostname, hostip) used by Travnet botnet for data upload, representing exfiltration over the C2 channel.
The rule identifies a Shiz Trojan C2 pattern: a GET to /login.php with a forged Google Referer and a legacy IE2.0 User-Agent, clearly showing command-and-control over HTTP.
The rule flags Chrome extension (.crx) downloads from non-Google sources (excluding googleusercontent, google.com, gvt1.com), indicating ingress tool transfer via malicious browser plugins.
The rule detects Firefox extension (.xpi) downloads from non-Mozilla domains, another case of ingress tool transfer through malicious browser add-ons.
The rule matches a URI pattern (/windows/update/search?hl=...) that mimics Windows Update traffic, demonstrating protocol or service impersonation by the Namihno Trojan.
The rule captures Cbeplay ransomware's abnormal HTTP POST with multipart/form-data, specific headers, and a file upload structure, indicative of data exfiltration over the C2 channel.
This rule focuses on the POST body of the same ransomware, looking for a numeric filename in the form data, further supporting exfiltration over C2.
The rule only detects HTML comment markers ('<!--ded509-->') left by a compromised site, which is an indicator of compromise but does not directly map to an observable ATT&CK technique.
The rule matches a Kazy Trojan check-in with a specific Opera User-Agent and a /count.php?page= URI, showing HTTP-based C2.
The rule identifies BlackRev v1 C2 traffic: a gate.php?reg= URI with a 10-character registration ID and a Synapse User-Agent, clearly command-and-control over web protocols.
Similar to the previous rule, this detects BlackRev v2 with a 15-character alphanumeric registration ID and an SEObot User-Agent, again HTTP C2.
This rule catches BlackRev v3 using a gate.php?id= parameter with a 15-character ID and an SEObot User-Agent, continuing the pattern of HTTP C2.
The rule matches a Kbot variant's s_alive.php?id= check-in URI, a straightforward HTTP C2 beacon.
The rule detects the companion s_task.php?id= URI used by the same Kbot variant for task retrieval, also HTTP C2.
The rule identifies Blocker Trojan traffic by its HTTP header structure: a GET to /index.html on a .info domain with a specific Cache-Control header and a generic User-Agent, all over HTTP.
The rule flags a POST request with 'cmd=gravar&dados=' (Portuguese for 'save data'), indicating the Blocker Trojan is exfiltrating data over its C2 channel.
